roadmap.goal: Ship slice 05 of ADO Epic #5775 (Story #5780): a Helm install cannot be made to run on a key nobody owns. With neither a key nor a secret holding one, the chart refuses to render, naming both. An external secret store owns the key, the container reads it from a mounted file rather than an environment variable, nothing in the chart can ever invent one, and a key an operator adds to that secret is picked up without a restart. The rotation this makes possible is four operator actions against their own store — add the new key alongside the old, watch the instance say it picked them up, ask it to re-encrypt, drop the old — and Lighthouse holds no write permission on any secret at any point.
roadmap.overview:
Six phases, 7 steps, one conventional commit each.

**Phase 01 (2 steps) is the backend half, and it goes first because it is the half with no chart in it.** The application already parses a mounted file — slice 01 shipped `MountedFileKeyRingSource`, and the roadmap that shipped it said in as many words: parsed here, watched in slice 05. This is that watch. Step 01-01 is the poller against an injected file source, so the whole case list — picked up, not-keys, empty, a key removed, unchanged content, no file named — is decided without a filesystem and without a boot. Step 01-02 is the one case an injected source cannot express: a real file replaced the way a kubelet replaces one, by writing a new directory and moving a link. That is the substrate lie ADR-153 names, and the only honest probe of it is a real link on a real filesystem.

**Phase 02 (1 step) is the render refusal, and the guard and the fix for what the guard breaks are one commit on purpose.** helm-unittest renders every template in the chart and only then selects the document under test, so an unconditional failure in `deployment-api.yaml` reds suites that never mention it — DEVOPS measured 46 of 56. The suite-level `set:` block that repairs that is five lines, and splitting it from the guard would mean deliberately pushing a red chart suite and repairing it in the next commit. They land together.

**Phase 03 (1 step) is custody itself** — the release-owned secret, the volume, the mount, the path in the ConfigMap, and the exclusion from the reloader. Its RED is the seven-case unit suite DEVOPS specified, which is also where the two enforcement assertions live: no environment variable name matches the key setting except the one carrying a path, and a tenant whose only managed credential is the encryption secret renders no reload annotation at all.

**Phase 04 (1 step) is CI parity**, which is not tidying-up here but the only place three scenarios can be decided at all: whether a real kubelet's projected file is readable by the non-root runtime user, whether the external-secret path survives a real install, and whether two identical renders are byte-identical. The standalone render gate and the kind smoke both break the moment the guard lands, so this phase cannot be deferred past phase 02 by more than the time it takes to write it.

**Phase 05 (1 step)** is the chart's own documentation and the version bump, which are one change because the drift gate and the publish guard both fail without the other.

**Phase 06 (1 step)** is the slice close: mutation, the Tenant Zero dogfood, and the verdict.

**Three things this roadmap decided that the upstream waves leave open.**

1. *The poll interval is configuration with a default, not a constant.* ADR-153 fixes 30 seconds and gives the reason (an operator's own round trip is longer than that). But a test that waits 30 seconds to prove a re-read is a test nobody runs, and a test that reaches into the poller to trigger a tick proves the tick and not the timer. The interval is therefore a setting with a 30-second default that the tests set to something small, which also gives an operator on a slow store a way out that is not a fork.

2. *The refusal lives in one named helper, not in each template that needs it.* The guard has to fire on `deployment-api.yaml` (which mounts the volume) and on `secret.yaml` (which may render the key) and must fire identically. Repeating the condition would let the two drift, and the drift would be silent — one template refusing and the other rendering is exactly the half-applied install the refusal exists to prevent. `_helpers.tpl` already carries `lighthouse.renderDbKeys` and `lighthouse.renderOidcKey`; this is the third of the same shape.

3. *Scenario 199 is already true and is confirmed rather than re-authored.* A credential stored under a key the ring no longer holds already reports unreadable on the connection and the field — that shipped in slice 01 and slice 04 and is asserted in `ConnectionValidationUnreadableSecretTests`. Step 01-02 confirms it still holds after a reload drops a key, which is the new path into it; it does not re-author the assertion.

**Estimate.** The slice brief carries ~5h, written before DISTILL produced 25 scenarios and before DEVOPS measured the helm-unittest blast radius. The step estimates below sum to ~14.5h. The brief's number is not corrected here; the gap is recorded so it is a known disagreement rather than a surprise at slice close.

slice_to_phase._not_in_this_roadmap_: the product documentation page, the security page and the compliance self-assessment, which are slice 06 (#5781); a driver where the key never enters the process at all, which the epic names as the successor; per-tenant rotation automation and the tenant ExternalSecret templates, which live in the private platform repository; migrating existing tenants onto their own keys, which is a platform operation this slice makes possible rather than performs.

phases.name: A key added while it is running
phases.description: The application already knows how to read a ring out of a mounted file; what it cannot do is notice that the file changed. Noticing is what makes an operator-owned rotation possible without a pod roll, and it is the reason the key is a file rather than an environment variable in the first place. Both guards keep the ring already in force, because the running ring is the only one known to work.

steps.name: Re-read the mounted keys, and refuse a change that will not read
steps.description: RED: author `KeyRingFileWatcherTests.cs` against an injected file source and a driven interval, so no case waits on a real timer. Cases: content that parses to a new ring replaces the ring in force and logs `encryption.keyring.reloaded` naming the ids it now holds; content that does not parse leaves the previous ring in force, logs at Error with the reason, and every stored secret still opens; content that parses to nothing at all is refused the same way; a reload that drops an id the ring currently holds is applied and logged at Warning naming the id that went away, because custody belongs to the operator; unchanged content re-read many times replaces nothing and logs nothing, so an operator is never told about a rotation that did not happen; no message written on any of those paths carries key material in any encoding, and the ones naming a key name only its id; and with no file configured the watcher does not start and nothing is ever read. GREEN: add `Services/Implementation/Encryption/KeyRingFileWatcher.cs` as a hosted service taking its file access, its clock interval and `IEncryptionKeyRingHolder` as injected capabilities. It compares a hash of the file's content rather than a timestamp — a kubelet moves a link rather than rewriting a file, and mtime on the path is not a reliable witness to either. It parses through the existing `KeyRingSerializer` and validates through the same path `MountedFileKeyRingSource` uses, so the file that is accepted at boot and the file that is accepted at reload are accepted by one piece of code. Register it only when `Encryption:KeysFile` is set. Add `Encryption:KeysReloadSeconds` defaulting to 30. COMMIT: `feat(encryption): notice a key the operator added without being restarted`.
red_to_green_tests: A new key in the file becomes the key in force, and is named in the log
Content that will not parse leaves the ring in force and logs the reason at Error
Content that parses to an empty ring is refused the same way
A reload that drops a held key is applied, and warns naming that key
Unchanged content re-read repeatedly replaces nothing and says nothing
No reload message carries key material in any encoding
With no file configured, nothing is read and the watcher never runs
criteria: Both refusal paths are fail-safe-old: the ring in force is never replaced by one that did not read.
The boot path and the reload path validate through the same code, so a file accepted at one is accepted at the other.
A Program.cs touch means the full backend Integration suite runs; the registration is conditional so no instance without a mounted file gains a background service.

steps.name: Prove it against the way a cluster actually replaces the file
steps.description: RED: author an integration probe against a real temp directory laid out the way a kubelet lays one out — a data directory, and the mounted path as a link into it. Cases: replacing the content by writing a new directory and moving the link is noticed on the next read, which is the case a subscription to the file would miss entirely because it would still be watching the old inode; and a credential stored under a key that a reload removed reports unreadable on the connection and on the field that holds it, with nothing sent to the work tracking system carrying it. The second case asserts an outcome that already ships — confirm it survives the new path into it rather than re-authoring the assertion that owns it. GREEN: whatever the probe shows is missing. If the hash comparison already covers it, this step lands the probe alone, and that is a complete step: the substrate lie is documented in ADR-153 and an undefended claim about it is worth less than a passing probe. COMMIT: `test(encryption): pin that a moved link is still noticed`.
red_to_green_tests: A link moved to a new directory is noticed on the next read
A credential on a key a reload removed reports unreadable rather than being tried
criteria: The probe uses a real link and a real move, because the failure it is about is a filesystem detail rather than a logic one.
It runs on Linux CI and skips nowhere silently: if the substrate cannot express a link, the test says so rather than passing.

phases.name: An install that names no key is refused
phases.description: The chart makes nothing, so an install that supplies nothing has to stop. It stops the way this chart already stops for a missing database password, because a security-relevant value a chart invents is a value nobody owns — and because refusing is the only shape that is also safe under the rendering path the platform itself uses, where asking the cluster what already exists always comes back empty.

steps.name: Refuse to render, and keep the existing suites green while doing it
steps.description: RED: add the refusal cases to a new `chart/tests/unit/encryption_test.yaml` — nothing supplied fails the render naming both values and carrying the command that makes a key; both supplied fails saying it cannot be both; and an install whose database and sign-in secrets are both externally owned still fails, which pins the guard as belonging to the install rather than to the shared secret's render condition. GREEN: add `lighthouse.requireEncryptionCustody` to `_helpers.tpl` as the single place the condition lives, and call it from both `deployment-api.yaml` and `secret.yaml` — repeating the condition would let the two drift, and one template refusing while the other renders is the half-applied install the refusal exists to prevent. Add the `encryption:` block to `values.yaml` and `values.schema.json` with both keys empty and neither defaulted. Then the part that is easy to discover expensively: helm-unittest renders every template before selecting the one under test, so this guard reds 46 of the 56 existing tests. Add a suite-level `set:` block supplying a fixture key to each of the five existing suites — five lines total, per-test overrides still work, and every existing exact failure-message assertion must keep matching, which is why the encryption guard is ordered after the frontend-mode and scaling assertions rather than before them. COMMIT: `feat(chart): refuse to install Lighthouse on a key nobody owns`.
red_to_green_tests: Nothing supplied fails the render, naming both ways forward
The message carries a command that makes a key
Supplying both a key and a secret fails, saying it cannot be both
An install whose other secrets are externally owned still fails
All 56 existing chart tests are green again
criteria: The condition exists once and is called twice; it is never written out twice.
helm unittest is green across all suites in the same commit that introduces the guard — no commit in this slice leaves the chart suite red.
helm lint stays green: lint neutralises a required value, and that is left exactly as it is rather than papered over with a --set, because hiding it would hide that lint never enforced this.

phases.name: The key the cluster owns arrives as a file
phases.description: Every other credential this chart hands the container travels as an environment variable, and this one deliberately does not: an environment variable is readable in a process dump and cannot change under a running process, so it would fail the requirement and make phase 01 impossible in the same stroke. The divergence is the point, and the chart has to say so in one sentence or somebody will align the two back.

steps.name: Mount the keys, and keep them out of everywhere else
steps.description: RED: complete `chart/tests/unit/encryption_test.yaml` with the four custody cases and the two enforcement assertions. With a key supplied: the release's own secret carries it and the volume points at the chart-owned name. With a secret named: zero encryption secret documents are rendered and the volume points at the operator's name. In either mode: the ConfigMap carries the path setting whose value is the mount path, no ConfigMap key and no container environment variable name matches the key setting other than that one, its value starts with a slash, and the mount is read-only with a mode the non-root runtime user can read. With only the named secret: no reload annotation and no configuration checksum is rendered at all, because the instance notices a new key by re-reading the file and rolling the pod for it would trade away the property the mount was chosen for. GREEN: render the encryption secret when a key is supplied; project the volume from whichever secret is in force; mount it read-only at the path; put the path setting in the ConfigMap alongside the other non-secret configuration, never in the Deployment's environment list; and leave `lighthouse.reloadSecrets` returning exactly the database and sign-in secrets. The mode is world-readable rather than owner-only on purpose: the runtime image ends on a non-root user, the chart sets no pod security context, and a projected file is owned by root — at owner-only the application cannot open its own keys and the pod crash-loops. The trust boundary is a pod running one process. COMMIT: `feat(chart): hand the encryption key to the container as a file it can only read`.
red_to_green_tests: A named secret renders no encryption secret of its own and the volume points at it
A supplied key is carried in the release's own secret
The mount is read-only and readable by the non-root runtime user
No container environment variable is key material; the one naming the keys carries a path
The non-secret configuration carries the path and nothing else about the keys
A tenant whose only managed credential is the encryption secret renders no reload annotation
The database credential and sign-in secret reach the container exactly as before
criteria: The two existing existingSecret idioms are unchanged in shape; only encryption travels the new way.
The named secret never joins the reloader's watch list.
The file mode is justified in one line where it is set, because the obvious tightening of it breaks the pod.

phases.name: The pipeline proves it against a real cluster
phases.description: Three of this slice's claims cannot be settled by rendering. Whether a real kubelet's projected file is readable by the non-root user is decided by a real kubelet; whether the externally-owned path works is decided by installing it; and whether an upgrade that changes nothing changes nothing is decided by diffing two renders. Two existing pipeline steps also break the moment the guard lands, so this phase follows phase 02 closely rather than at leisure.

steps.name: Repair what the guard breaks, and add the two gates and the missing install
steps.description: RED: the pipeline itself is the test. The standalone render gate and the kind smoke both fail as soon as phase 02 lands, and the externally-owned install has never been exercised against a real kubelet at all. GREEN: supply a fixture key to the standalone render gate and to the kind install; add a second install into the same cluster that creates a secret first and names it, so the path Tenant Zero actually uses is exercised by a real kubelet and both volume resolutions are covered; add a shell gate asserting no template invents a value anywhere near an encryption value; add a render-determinism gate rendering the chart twice with identical values and diffing the two byte for byte; and add a commented, REQUIRED-marked encryption block to `values-enterprise.yaml` in the shape the database password and the sign-in secret are already presented there. Leave `helm lint` alone. COMMIT: `ci(chart): install both custody modes into a real cluster and pin the render`.
red_to_green_tests: The standalone render gate is green again with a key supplied
The kind install is green again, proving the projected file is readable by the non-root user
A second install naming an operator-created secret becomes ready and serves its page
No template invents a value near an encryption value
Two identical renders are byte-identical
criteria: helm lint is not 'fixed' with a --set: it never enforced this, and hiding that would hide it further.
Both installs go into the same cluster, so the second costs a secret and an install rather than a second cluster.
A pod that cannot find its named secret is visible in the diagnostics dump rather than only as a timeout.

phases.name: The chart says what it now needs
phases.description: An operator meets this slice as one more required flag on their first command. What makes that affordable is the failure message and the README saying the same thing, and the README saying in one sentence why encryption travels differently from the database password — otherwise somebody will align them back and undo the reason the mount exists.

steps.name: Document the three custody modes, the rotation, and bump the chart
steps.description: GREEN: describe the three modes in the values comments — a key supplied directly, a secret an external store owns, and nothing supplied, which is refused. Regenerate `chart/README.md` with helm-docs and commit it in the same change, because the drift gate fails on a stale README and the generated half cannot be hand-written. Add the new flag to the quick-start snippets in `README.md.gotmpl` by hand, since those are not generated. Write the four-action rotation into the README: add the new key as the first entry alongside the old, wait for the instance to log that it picked them up or roll the pod, ask for the re-encryption from the encryption panel, then drop the old key — and say plainly that Lighthouse writes to no secret at any point and needs no permission to. Add the one sentence about why the encryption key travels as a file when the database password does not. Bump `Chart.yaml` version; if the application image is re-pinned in the same change, appVersion and the enterprise values image tag move together, because the publish guard asserts they agree. Use the seeded terminology defaults throughout. COMMIT: `docs(chart): describe the three ways to own the encryption key, and how to rotate it`.
red_to_green_tests: The README drift gate is green against the regenerated file
The quick-start snippets carry the new flag
The publish version guard is satisfied by the bump
criteria: The generated README is regenerated, never hand-edited.
The rotation is written as four operator actions with what to look at between them.
The product documentation page, the security page and the compliance self-assessment are slice 06 and are not touched here.

phases.name: Slice close
phases.description: The dogfood is the slice's own learning hypothesis: refusing is affordable, disproved if a self-hoster following the README cannot get to a working install as easily as before. The Tenant Zero half also carries the two soft KPIs, which nothing in CI can measure.

steps.name: Mutation, dogfood, verdict
steps.description: Run Stryker.NET over the backend surface this slice adds, using `mutation/stryker.5780.backend.json`; the chart carries no mutable code and its equivalent is the seven-case suite plus the two shell gates. Then the dogfood, in order: confirm an install with no encryption values refuses to render, naming both; install into Tenant Zero naming its own secret; save a Connection; run three consecutive upgrades with unchanged values and confirm the Connection still syncs after each; then walk the four-action rotation end to end and confirm nothing was re-entered, recording the wall-clock against the 60-second budget. Record the verdict — confirmed or disproved — in the slice brief, and append the walkthrough to `verification/manual-walkthrough.md`. Move Story #5780 to Resolved once CI is green and the dogfood is recorded; the Epic stays Active, because Closed here means released.
steps.scenario_name: All slice-05 scenarios, end to end
red_to_green_tests: Backend mutation kill rate is at or above 80% on the changed surface
A no-encryption install refuses to render on Tenant Zero's own path
Three consecutive upgrades leave every Connection syncing
The four-action rotation completes with zero credentials re-entered
criteria: The tenant's secret exists before the tenant's chart version is bumped, or the render fails and the sync stops.
The verdict is recorded either way; a disproved hypothesis is a result, and the thing to fix is the README.
The Epic is not closed.
